questions.stem: You are examining Mr Tan, a 36-year-old fisherman in the ED, whose left ring finger DIP joint became hot, swollen and painful overnight. Fishermen are at risk of hand infections, so you check for flexor sheath infection as well as joint disease. Which finding would most suggest flexor tenosynovitis rather than a DIP joint problem?
options: Tenderness localised to the DIP joint line itself on gentle palpation of the joint
Erythema and swelling confined to the dorsum of the DIP joint
Severe pain along the volar finger on passive extension of the finger
Fluctuant swelling and redness along the lateral nail fold
questions.why: Pain on passive extension is the most specific of Kanavel's signs for flexor sheath infection. The others are a finger held flexed, swelling of the whole finger and tenderness along the sheath. Flexor sheath infection is a surgical emergency.
notes: Tenderness that stays at the joint line points to the joint itself, as in gout or septic arthritis, not to the tendon sheath.
Redness and swelling confined to the DIP joint fit a monoarthritis; sheath infection makes the whole finger swell along the volar side.
A fluctuant, red nail fold is a paronychia, a superficial infection of the nail fold, not an infection of the flexor sheath.

questions.stem: Mr Tan, 36, has had his second gout attack, confirmed by urate crystals on aspirate. At GP review after the flare has settled, he agrees to start allopurinol with flare prophylaxis. He has no tophi on examination and his eGFR is above 90. What target should his allopurinol be titrated to?
options: Serum urate below 0.36 mmol/L, starting allopurinol low and titrating up
Serum urate below 0.42 mmol/L, the upper limit of the lab reference range
Serum urate below 0.30 mmol/L, starting allopurinol low and titrating up
Serum urate below 0.48 mmol/L, the level above which gout risk climbs steeply
questions.why: Australian guidance (eTG, RACGP) sets a treat-to-target urate below 0.36 mmol/L for gout without tophi. Allopurinol is started at a low dose and increased every few weeks until the target is reached. Below this level crystals dissolve and attacks stop.
notes: The lab upper limit is above the urate saturation point (about 0.40 mmol/L), so crystals would keep forming; being 'in range' is not the goal.
A lower target of below 0.30 mmol/L is kept for tophaceous or severe gout, and Mr Tan has no tophi.
At 0.48 mmol/L urate is well above saturation, so this target would not dissolve crystals or prevent attacks.

questions.stem: Mr Tan, 36, has acute gout of his left ring finger DIP joint, confirmed by needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals on aspirate. Yet his serum urate taken during the flare is 0.40 mmol/L, within the lab reference range. What best explains a normal serum urate during an acute gout flare?
options: Xanthine oxidase activity in the liver falls during the acute inflammatory response phase
Acute-phase proteins increase urate reabsorption in the renal tubules
Activated neutrophils convert uric acid to allantoin in the circulation
Inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 increase the kidney's fractional excretion of urate
questions.why: In an acute flare, systemic inflammation (IL-6) increases renal urate excretion, and urate is also being laid down as crystals. Both lower serum urate, so a normal level does not exclude gout. Repeat it 2 to 4 weeks after the flare.
notes: A fall in xanthine oxidase activity in the liver is not the recognised mechanism; the drop in serum urate is mainly from increased excretion by the kidney.
This is the wrong way round: more tubular reabsorption would raise serum urate, not lower it.
Humans have no uricase, so urate cannot be turned into allantoin; that is why humans get gout and most other mammals do not.

questions.stem: Before a joint procedure on Mr Tan's left ring finger DIP joint, a digital nerve block is planned for analgesia. The block needs to cover sensation to the skin around the distal ring finger, including its dorsum. Which nerves provide sensation to this area?
options: The ulnar nerve alone, through its palmar and dorsal digital branches
The median nerve to the radial half and the ulnar nerve to the ulnar half
The median nerve alone, through its common palmar digital branches
The radial nerve to the dorsum and the median nerve to the volar surface of the finger
questions.why: The ring finger is split: the median nerve supplies its radial half and the ulnar nerve its ulnar half. Their palmar digital branches also curve dorsally to supply the nail bed and the dorsum of the distal phalanx. A digital block must therefore reach both sides of the finger.
notes: The ulnar nerve supplies only the ulnar half of the ring finger; the radial half belongs to the median nerve.
The median nerve supplies only the radial half of the ring finger, so blocking it alone leaves the ulnar side with sensation.
The radial nerve's dorsal branches stop around the proximal phalanx; the palmar digital nerves supply the dorsum at the DIP joint.
